query: For additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 high-entropy alloy with an fcc matrix, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs degradation during elevated-temperature exposure to oxidizing or reducing gases and why catastrophic failure may occur? Specify a controlled change that would reveal the governing behavior, predicted observations relative to the starting-state baseline, applicable exposure boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a clear falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: In the AM Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 HEA, degradation at elevated temperatures is governed by aggressive grain‐boundary diffusion that accelerates the formation of a mixed (Al-, Cr- and Ti-containing) oxide scale. The rapid, nonuniform oxide growth creates internal stresses and local decohesion at grain boundaries, which leads to spallation of the protective layer and eventual catastrophic failure.
generation.material_initial_state: As-printed Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 with a fine-grained FCC microstructure and high grain boundary density resulting from rapid solidification during additive manufacturing.
generation.intervention: Implement a controlled post-process heat treatment (moderate annealing) to coarsen the grain structure and reduce the grain boundary density before exposing the samples to elevated temperature under oxidizing and reducing conditions.
generation.conditions: Exposure at temperatures between 850 °C and 1050 °C for durations up to 100 hours, under both oxidizing (e.g., O2-rich) and reducing (e.g., H2-containing) gas atmospheres.
generation.structural_mediator: Grain boundary density and associated defect sites that serve as fast diffusion paths for oxygen (or reactive reducing species), thus mediating the kinetics of oxide formation and subsequent stress buildup.
generation.mechanism: High grain boundary density promotes rapid diffusion of ambient species into the bulk, leading to the formation of a multi-layer oxide scale (e.g., mixed Al2O3, Cr2O3, and Ti oxides) that initially may offer some protection but eventually grows nonuniformly. The mismatch in mechanical properties and volumetric changes between the oxide and metal phases induces internal stresses that cause cracking and spallation of the scale, exposing fresh metal and accelerating degradation. In reducing environments, the inability to form a stable protective oxide similarly permits internal degradation through uncontrolled oxidation/reduction reactions.
generation.predicted_outcome: Samples retaining the as-printed fine-grained microstructure will exhibit accelerated oxidation kinetics, thicker but more cracked and non-adherent oxide scales, and early onset of catastrophic failure. In contrast, annealed samples with coarser grains (and lower grain boundary density) are expected to form thinner, more continuous oxide layers and exhibit slower degradation and improved high-temperature stability.
generation.baseline: The as-printed state with a fine grain structure exhibiting rapid oxide buildup and associated internal stress leading to spallation and failure.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis applies to exposures in the 850–1050 °C range under oxidizing or reducing atmospheres; behavior outside this temperature range or under inert conditions may differ.
generation.uncertainty: The precise role of Ti in modifying the stability and adhesion of the oxide scale and the quantitative differences in oxidation kinetics between microstructures remain to be fully defined.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 samples: one kept as-printed and one subjected to a post-process annealing treatment to coarsen the grains. Expose each set to 900 °C under an oxidizing atmosphere (O2-rich) and a reducing gas mixture for up to 100 hours. Monitor the evolution of the oxide scale, internal oxidation, and the mechanical integrity (via fracture analysis) during and after exposure.
measurements: Oxide scale thickness and continuity (using SEM/XRD)
Extent of spallation or cracking (via post-mortem microscopy)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the annealed (coarser grain) samples do not show reduced oxidation kinetics, more adherent oxide scales, and improved failure resistance relative to as-printed samples, or if the degradation behavior is independent of the grain boundary density change under the specified conditions, then the hypothesis is falsified.

AbstractThe oxidation behavior of an equimolar Cr-Mn-Fe-Co high-entropy alloy (HEA) processed by 3D laser printing was investigated at 700 °C and 900 °C. The oxidation kinetics of the alloy followed the parabolic rate law, and the oxidation rate constant increased with the rising of the temperature. Inward diffusion of oxygen and outward diffusion of cations took place during the high-temperature oxidation process. A spinel-type oxide was formed on the surface, and the thickness of the oxide layer increased with the rising of experimental temperature or time. The exfoliation of the oxide layer took place when the test was operated at 900 °C over 12 h. During oxidation tests, the matrix was propped open by oxides and was segmented into small pieces. The formation of loose structures had great effects on the high-temperature oxidation resistance of the HEA.Keywords: metals and alloys, 3D printing, oxidation

AbstractThis work investigates the effect of ultrafine-grain microstructure on the oxidation behavior of AlCoCrFeNi high entropy alloy (HEA). The ultrafine-grain microstructure is obtained using stationary friction processing performed at two different rotational speeds, 400 and 1800 rpm, for 5 min duration. Processed samples demonstrate high depth of refinement (DOR) and ultrafine grain size (0.43–1 μm) at high rotational speeds along with significant phase transformations from BCC/B2 to FCC microstructure. Further, surface free energy of the ultrafine-grain microstructure is enhanced up to 35%. Oxidation kinetics of the ultrafine-grained sample is decelerated up to 12–48% in a temperature range of 850–1050 °C for a duration of 100 h. Chromia and alumina were the predominant oxides formed in almost all the samples oxidized at elevated temperature. In addition, spinel Co(Cr,Fe)2O4/Fe(Co,Cr)2O4 formation is also detected in the unprocessed oxidized samples. Processed samples rich in grain boundaries (GBs) promote internal oxidation to form Al-rich inner oxides. Chen et al. investigated the effect of Si (0.3 atom %) content on the oxidation behavior of the Al0.6CrFeCoNi HEA and found that the oxidation kinetics of the Si-containing HEA was lower than that of the Al0.6CrFeCoNi HEA at lower temperatures (800 and 900 °C) but became inferior compared to Al0.6CrFeCoNi at the higher temperature of 1000 °C. Lu et al. reported the effect of Al content on the oxidation behavior of Y/Hf-doped AlxCoCrFeNi (x = 0.7, 1, 1.3) high-entropy alloys. Al0.7CoCrFeNi showed the lowest oxidation resistance owing to the formation of an outer spinel layer with an inner Al2O3 layer, followed by AlCoCrFeNi due to the formation of protective Al2O3 scale and Al1.3CoCrFeNi exhibiting the highest resistance to oxidation. While the major focus of prior studies has been on the development of new alloy systems, there are only a few studies on limiting the high temperature oxidation via tailoring the material’s microstructure.
